title: 'Sadly, Cricket Wasn’t Part of It Then': Harmanpreet Kaur Sets Her Sights on LA 2028
excerpt: India’s World Cup-winning captain invoked Milkha Singh’s legacy as she spoke about her dream of leading the country at cricket’s Olympic debut in Los Angeles — a city where millions of Indian Americans could watch it happen.
body:
Harmanpreet Kaur grew up in Moga, a small city in Punjab, watching athletes from her state board flights to the Olympics. Milkha Singh, the Flying Sikh, was the standard. Sprinters, wrestlers, and hockey players followed. Cricket, though — the sport she had chosen — never made the list.

That changes in two years. Cricket returns to the Olympic programme in 2028 for the first time since 1900, when a single exhibition match was played in Paris. The T20 format will be contested at the Los Angeles Games, and Harmanpreet Kaur, the 37-year-old captain who led India to the 2025 Women’s ODI World Cup title, has made it clear she intends to be there.

“Growing up, I heard a lot about Milkha Singh — he was a great athlete from Punjab,” Harmanpreet said in an interview published by the Olympic Games’ official account this week. “There were so many other athletes from Punjab who were part of the Olympics and won medals for our country. It was a dream that one day I wanted to represent India in an Olympic sport. Sadly, at that time cricket wasn’t part of it. But now we have a great opportunity.”

## A Once-in-a-Career Chance

The timing is both poetic and precarious. Harmanpreet will be 39 when the Los Angeles Games begin in July 2028. She is already the most capped T20I player in the history of Indian women’s cricket, having crossed 200 appearances during the ongoing Women’s T20 World Cup in England. Her body of work — a World Cup title, multiple ICC tournament campaigns, and a career that has spanned nearly 15 years at the international level — would make her a fitting flag-bearer for cricket’s Olympic return.

But she will have to earn her place. The Indian selectors will face difficult choices by 2028, with younger players pressing for spots and the demands of the T20 format favouring athleticism and power hitting. Whether Harmanpreet is part of the Olympic squad will depend on her form over the next two years, a stretch that includes the ongoing T20 World Cup, bilateral series, and the Women’s Premier League.

“I think it is a very big thing,” she said. “If you do well there, you will be remembered forever. People are going to remember your entire life.”

## Why LA Matters for the Diaspora

The choice of Los Angeles as the host city gives the tournament an unmistakable diaspora dimension. Southern California is home to one of the largest Indian-American communities in the United States. The greater Los Angeles area, from Artesia’s Little India to the tech corridors of Irvine, has a South Asian population that numbers in the hundreds of thousands. Cricket in LA is not a novelty — it is played in parks across the region, watched in living rooms tuned to Willow and JioCinema, and debated in group chats that span time zones.

When the T20 competition begins at the 2028 Olympics, it will be the first time many NRIs can watch India play cricket at a global multi-sport event without leaving their city. The prospect of Harmanpreet Kaur — or her successors — playing under the Olympic rings at a venue a freeway exit from the Swaminarayan Mandir in Chino Hills carries a weight that no bilateral series or even a World Cup can fully replicate.

Cricket’s 128-year absence from the Olympics has meant that generations of Indian fans have had to compartmentalise their sporting passions. They watch the Olympics for hockey, shooting, wrestling, and badminton. They watch cricket separately, on a different calendar, in a different ecosystem. LA 2028 merges those two worlds for the first time.

## The Road From Lord’s to Los Angeles

Before any of that materialises, Harmanpreet has immediate business. India face Australia at Lord’s on Sunday in what amounts to a virtual quarterfinal of the Women’s T20 World Cup. Australia are unbeaten in four matches. India, with three wins and one loss, need a victory to secure their place in the semi-finals.

The equation is simple but the opponent is not. Australia have dominated women’s cricket for the better part of two decades, and their record in ICC knockout matches against India is formidable. Harmanpreet’s squad will need to be at their best.

“We know they are a strong team, but we also know we have the ability to match them,” Harmanpreet said ahead of the match. “It’s only about what we can do.”

If India go deep in this tournament, it will only strengthen the case for Harmanpreet’s Olympic candidacy. A World Cup-winning captain leading the country on cricket’s Olympic debut, in a city where the Indian tricolour hangs from storefronts along Pioneer Boulevard — few stories in Indian sport would write themselves quite so neatly.
